title: Fluency Instruction Part 2
author: Shanahan, Timothy
summary: Timothy Shanahan follows up his previous post by describing how to implement fluency instruction effectively at the secondary level. Reviewing the Landreth and Young (2021) study, he identifies five features that produced comprehension gains: using appealing texts, replacing round-robin reading with choral and paired repeated reading, setting Friday performance goals to reinforce prosody rather than speed, providing parsed text showing phrase boundaries, and using teacher modeling only for difficult passages. Shanahan argues that because fluency correlates strongly with comprehension in early grades but the relationship attenuates as students approach the 175–200 WCPM ceiling, roughly 40–50% of secondary students still benefit from explicit fluency instruction. He proposes fluency work as a cross-disciplinary shared commitment, with each content teacher providing 10 minutes of practice per week using the texts of their own course—enough to meaningfully accelerate progress without displacing content.
points: Oral reading fluency correlates strongly with comprehension in early grades but the relationship attenuates as students reach the 175–200 WCPM ceiling; secondary schools should focus instruction on the 40–50% of students still below target.

The best fluency study for older students (Landreth & Young, 2021) used student-selected texts, choral and paired repeated reading, Friday performance presentations, and deliberately de-emphasized speed in favor of prosody.

Round-robin reading is wasteful—only one student reads at a time, anxiety is heightened, and there is rarely rereading to improve performance; choral and paired reading eliminate the social risk while maximizing practice volume.
Parsed text—marking phrase boundaries for students to practice on—improves both prosody and comprehension, and having students parse texts themselves generates productive discussion of meaning.

Fluency instruction should be a cross-disciplinary commitment with each content teacher providing short weekly practice using the texts of their own course, so no teacher must reduce instructional focus on their subject.
quotes: Text reading fluency is a necessary, but insufficient condition for comprehension. If you can’t read a text fluently, you’re unlikely to get much from it.

Fluency is a combination of accuracy (reading the words as printed), automaticity (accomplishing this reading without conscious attention), and prosody (making the reading sound like language). As such, speed is an imperfect indicator of automaticity.
A fast reading rate suggests that kids are translating print to language without much effort; effort that may distract from comprehension. But fast reading is not the goal.

having one student reading something aloud while everyone else listens or supposedly follows along. That approach is wasteful. No one gets much fluency practice that way; only one student reads at a time, and if it doesn’t go well, there is rarely any rereading to improve the performance.
When half the class is reading simultaneously, embarrassment disappears like magic.
Practicing with such texts should foster both fluency improvement and increased academic knowledge.

it would be even more doable, however, if all the academic teachers accepted this as a shared responsibility, with each department signing on to provide some number of minutes to these kinds of activities each week with the texts of their curriculum.
Too many kids are slipping through the reading cracks in secondary school, undermining their chances for academic success.
